source_text: Quid expectamus amplius? tenemus enim, quod iuxta latus erat. quomodo libet iam fingite figuras et qualialibet liniamenta describite, moles certe illa inmensa terrae tenebrarum aut recto latere adiungebatur terrae lucis aut curuo aut tortuoso. sed si tortuoso, et illa sancta terra tortuosum habet latus; nam si ipsa rectum habet latus et tortuoso huius latere tangitur, interpatent cauernae quaedam profundae per infinitum inanes nec iam supra terram tantum tenebrarum inanitas erat, sicut audire solebamus. quod si ita est, quanto melius erat, ut se aliquanto longius terra luminis remoueret atque illa inanitas tanta interesset, ne omnino posset a tenebrarum terra ulla ex parte contingi! immo etiam tantum spatium pateret inanis profunditatis, ut si qua gentis illius oreretur inprobitas, etiamsi temere transilire in illam uellent principes tenebrarum — quoniam nec uolare posunt corpora, \' nisi aere corporeo subportentur —, per illud inane praecipitati et, quia infinitum deorsum uersus esset, ad nullum aliquando fundum peruenientes, etiamsi semper possent uiuere, numquam tamen, dum deorsum semper feruntur, possent nocere. si autem curuo latere adiungebatur, terra quoque lucis curuo eam sinu deformiter recipiebat. aut si introrsus ista quasi specie theatri curua erat, curuam terrae luminis partem tali sinu receptam non minus deformi copulatione amplectebatur. aut si ista curuum habebat latus et illa rectum, non ex toto eam latere adtingebat. et utique melius erat, sicut supra dixi, ut nulla ex parte contingeret tantumque inane interesset, ut et iusto interuallo utramque terram seiungeret et temerarios inprobos per infinitum praecipites nihil nocere permitteret. quodsi recto latere latus rectum adtingebat, non uideo quidem aliqua uel receptacula uel hiatus, sed plane uideo tantam pacem tantamque secum terrae utriusque concordiam, ut maior coniunctio esse non possit. quid enim speciosius, quid conuenientius quam rectum recto ita copulari, ut nulla ex parte sinus aliquis uel flexus disrumpat aut dirimat naturalem ac stabilem per infinitum spatium loci et ab infinita aeternitate iuncturam ? quae recta latera utriusque terrae, etiamsi interposito inani separarentur, non solum per se ipsa pulchra essent, quia tam recta essent, sed interiecto quoque interuallo ita sibi congruerent, ut hinc atque illinc pariles rectitudines etiamsi nulla coniunctione, ipsa tamen similitudine in unam pulchritudinem conuenirent. cum autem accedit ista coniunctio, quid concordius et pacatius hac utraque terra, quid uero etiam ipsa copulatione duorum rectorum laterum pulchrius dici aut cogitari possit, non inuenio.
thought_title: The geometry of the two lands refutes Mani's myth
orientation: Augustine is examining Mani's Fundamental Letter, where Mani says the land of darkness lay along one side and flank of the land of light, and now Augustine presses the spatial implications of that claim.
pass_a_gloss: What more do we wait for? For we hold that it was alongside the side. However you like, now invent shapes and describe lineaments of whatever sort, certainly that immense mass of the land of darkness was joined to the land of light either by a straight side or by a curved or twisted one. But if by a twisted one, then also that holy land has a twisted side; for if it itself has a straight side and is touched by the twisted side of this one, certain deep caverns lie open between them, empty through the infinite, and no longer was there emptiness only above the land of darkness, as we used to hear. But if this is so, how much better it was that the land of light should remove itself somewhat farther away and that so great an emptiness should lie between, so that it could not be touched at all by the land of darkness from any part! Indeed even so great a space of empty depth would lie open, that if any shamelessness of that people should arise, even if the princes of darkness should wish to leap rashly into that land — since bodies cannot fly unless they are supported by bodily air —, they would be hurled headlong through that emptiness and, because it would be infinite in the downward direction, they would never arrive at any bottom, and even if they could always live, nevertheless they could never do harm, while they are always carried downward. But if it was joined by a curved side, the land of light also received it deformedly in a curved hollow. Or if that one was curved inward like the shape of a theater, it embraced the curved part of the land of light received in such a hollow with a no less deformed coupling. Or if that one had a curved side and that one a straight side, it did not touch it with its whole side. And certainly it was better, as I said above, that it should touch it from no part and that so great an emptiness should lie between, so that it both separated each land by a just interval and allowed the rash shameless ones, hurled headlong through the infinite, to do no harm. But if a straight side touched a straight side, I do not see indeed any receptacles or gaps, but I plainly see so great a peace and so great a concord of each land with the other, that a greater joining cannot exist. For what is more beautiful, what more fitting than for a straight thing to be coupled to a straight thing in such a way that no hollow or bend from any part breaks apart or separates the natural and stable joining through infinite space of place and from infinite eternity? The straight sides of each land, even if they were separated by an intervening emptiness, would not only be beautiful through themselves, because they were so straight, but also with an interval placed between they would so agree with each other, that equal straightnesses on this side and on that side, even with no joining, would nevertheless come together into one beauty by their very likeness. But when this joining is added, what is more concordant and more peaceful than each of these lands, and what indeed more beautiful than the very coupling of two straight sides could be said or thought, I do not find.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for Mani's realm of evil.
Fixed glossary term for Mani's realm of God; the source alternates between 'lucis' and 'luminis', both rendered by the same glossary English.
Renders the moral quality of the hypothetical attack by the princes of darkness; 'shamelessness' keeps the sense of brazen wrongdoing.
Standard rendering for the rulers of Mani's land of darkness; keeps the political-military metaphor Augustine is using.
Renders the noun from 'iungo' for the contact between the two lands; 'joining' keeps the spatial and physical sense.
Keeps the abstract noun 'rectitudines' as 'straightnesses' to preserve Augustine's point about the quality of being straight as a beauty.

pass_b_english: What more are we waiting for? We have it in our grasp: we hold what was alongside the side. Now invent whatever shapes you like and sketch whatever outlines you please, but that immense mass of the land of darkness was certainly joined to the land of light either by a straight side, or a curved one, or a twisted one. But if it was twisted, then the holy land also has a twisted side. For if the holy land has a straight side and is touched by the twisted side of the other, deep caverns lie open between them, empty through infinite space, and the emptiness was no longer only above the land of darkness, as we used to hear. And if that is so, how much better it would have been for the land of light to withdraw a little farther away and let so great an emptiness lie between, so that it could not be touched by the land of darkness on any side at all! Indeed, so great a space of empty depth would lie open that if any shamelessness arose from that nation—even if the princes of darkness recklessly wished to leap across to it, since bodies cannot fly unless they are supported by bodily air—they would be hurled headlong through that emptiness, and because it would be infinite in the downward direction, they would never reach any bottom. Even if they could live forever, they could never do harm while they were always being carried downward. But if it was joined by a curved side, then the land of light received it in a curved hollow, and that was a deformed embrace. Or if the other land was curved inward like the shape of a theater, it clasped the curved part of the land of light in such a hollow with a coupling no less deformed. Or if the one had a curved side and the other a straight one, it did not touch it along the whole side. And certainly it would have been better, as I said above, for it not to touch on any side, and for so much emptiness to lie between that it would separate the two lands by a proper interval and allow the reckless and shameless, hurled headlong through the infinite, to do no harm. But if a straight side touched a straight side, I do not see any receptacles or gaps, but I plainly see such great peace and such great concord between the two lands that no greater joining could exist. For what is more beautiful, what more fitting, than for straight to be coupled to straight in such a way that no hollow or bend anywhere breaks or divides a natural and stable joining through infinite space and from infinite eternity? The straight sides of both lands, even if they were separated by an intervening emptiness, would not only be beautiful in themselves because they were so straight, but with the interval placed between they would correspond to each other in such a way that the equal straightnesses on this side and that, even without any joining, would come together into one beauty by their very likeness. But when this joining is added, what could be more harmonious and peaceful than these two lands, and what more beautiful than the very coupling of two straight sides could be said or thought? I cannot find it.

problems.source_quote: tenemus enim, quod iuxta latus erat
problems.why: Missing 'we hold/grasp' and misrendering 'quod' as 'it was' rather than 'what'—the sense is 'we hold what was alongside the side'
problems.fix: we hold what was alongside the side

problems.quote: the emptiness was no longer only above the land of darkness
problems.source_quote: nec iam supra terram tantum tenebrarum inanitas erat
problems.why: Misreads 'nec iam' as 'was no longer' instead of 'nor was the emptiness now only above'—the point is that caverns extend in other directions too, not that emptiness ceased
problems.fix: nor was the emptiness now only above the land of darkness
problems.ruling: 'was no longer' misreads 'nec iam'; sense is 'nor was the emptiness now only above'—caverns extend elsewhere, emptiness didn't cease.

edits.old: We have it in our grasp: it was alongside the side.
edits.new: We have it in our grasp: we hold what was alongside the side.

edits.old: and the emptiness was no longer only above the land of darkness
edits.new: nor was the emptiness now only above the land of darkness

fixed: Corrected 'it was alongside the side' to 'we hold what was alongside the side' to render 'tenemus enim, quod iuxta latus erat' accurately.

Corrected 'the emptiness was no longer only above the land of darkness' to 'nor was the emptiness now only above the land of darkness' to render 'nec iam supra terram tantum tenebrarum inanitas erat' accurately.

problems.quote: since bodies cannot fly unless they are supported by bodily air
problems.why: Missing negative: 'nec volare possunt' = 'nor can bodies fly.' English 'cannot fly' loses the 'nor' connection to previous clause, weakening logical structure.
problems.fix: since bodies cannot fly, nor can they unless supported by bodily air

problems.quote: nor was the emptiness now only above the land of darkness, as we used to hear
problems.source_quote: nec iam supra terram tantum tenebrarum inanitas erat, sicut audire solebamus
problems.why: Misreads 'nec iam...tantum' ('and no longer only above'); English 'nor was...now only' flips meaning to say emptiness WAS only above, opposite of source.
problems.fix: and the emptiness was no longer only above the land of darkness, as we used to hear.
problems.ruling: 'nec iam...tantum' = 'no longer only'; English 'nor was...now only' says emptiness WAS only above, reversing source meaning.

edits.old: since bodies cannot fly unless they are supported by bodily air
edits.new: since bodies cannot fly, nor can they unless they are supported by bodily air

edits.old: nor was the emptiness now only above the land of darkness, as we used to hear
edits.new: and the emptiness was no longer only above the land of darkness, as we used to hear

fixed: Fixed 'since bodies cannot fly unless they are supported by bodily air' to 'since bodies cannot fly, nor can they unless they are supported by bodily air' to restore the negative connection from 'nec volare possunt'.

Fixed 'nor was the emptiness now only above the land of darkness, as we used to hear' to 'and the emptiness was no longer only above the land of darkness, as we used to hear' to match 'nec iam...tantum' meaning 'and no longer only'.

problems.quote: nor can they unless they are supported by bodily air
problems.why: English adds 'nor can they' which is not in source; Latin only says bodies cannot fly unless supported by bodily air.
problems.fix: since bodies cannot fly unless they are supported by bodily air

edits.old: since bodies cannot fly, nor can they unless they are supported by bodily air
edits.new: since bodies cannot fly unless they are supported by bodily air

fixed: Removed 'nor can they' from 'since bodies cannot fly, nor can they unless they are supported by bodily air'; the source 'nisi aere corporeo subportentur' means 'unless they are supported by bodily air' without the added clause.

dismissed.quote: the emptiness was no longer only above the land of darkness
dismissed.why: Misreads 'nec iam' as 'no longer' instead of 'nor was'; flips meaning—emptiness is between lands, not gone from above
dismissed.note: 'nec iam ... tantum ... erat' does mean the emptiness was no longer only above the land of darkness; the English is correct.
